• Scientific name: Stenopus hispidus
  • Other names: Cleaner shrimp, Boxer shrimp, Barber pole shrimp, Candy cane shrimp, Banded prawns, Clown shrimp
  • Minimum tank size: 20 gallons (~90 litres)
  • Breeding: Difficult
  • Water type: SG 1.023–1.025
  • Optimal KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: Omnivore
  • Temperament: Aggressive (territorial)
  • Colour: bright red bars banding its white body

The coral banded shrimp is one of the most popular decapods in the marine aquarium trade because of its bright coloration and hardiness. It is a reef-associated cleaner shrimp with a worldwide distribution. It is known to remove and eat ectoparasites, injured or dead tissue and excess food particles from fishes. It is fairly easy to care for, even for beginners.
Coral banded shrimp occur in the Indo-Pacific region, the Red Sea and the Western Atlantic Ocean, where stocks are heavily collected to meet the demand of the marine ornamental trade.

This species inhabits rocky or coralline areas from a depth of a few centimetres to at least 30 metres. Adults are found in crevices or overhangs in reefs and are thought to move over an extremely limited area (less than 1 m2), with males showing territorial behaviour within this area.

In the natural environment, adults are typically found in mating pairs on coral reefs.
It is recommended to have at least a 20-gallon (~90 litres) tank when planning to buy them. They are too big for smaller tanks.

Coral banded shrimp are hardy animals that are often the first invertebrate for many beginning marine aquarists.

Molting is necessary for any shrimp to grow. According to research:

  • They grow rapidly during the first 30 weeks, gradually slowing, and essentially stop after approximately 50 weeks (~1 year).
  • Molt interval increases and growth increments decline as body size increases.
  • In general, the inter-molt duration is about 22–26 days (adults).
  • There is no significant difference in inter-molt intervals between males and females.
  • Mortality is size specific. Large shrimp have higher survival rates than smaller individuals; the probability of survival increases by approximately 6% per 1 mm increase in body size.

They generally live between 2 and 5 years in proper conditions.

They can live only in marine aquariums. Temperature should be between 24–27°C, SG 1.024–1.026. Coral banded shrimp prefer pH 8.0–8.4 and KH 8–9.

Do not forget to acclimatise them before putting them into the tank. Without proper acclimation, there is a higher risk of the shrimp dying from shock.
Preferably, the aquarium should have beach sand as a substrate and some rock for shelter.

Coral banded shrimp are omnivores. They eat meat (pieces of fish, shrimp, squid, shellfish and so on), flakes and pellets.

Give them a variety of food, from flake food to frozen or live food, so they get all the necessary microelements. Feed them at least three times a week.

Do not let them go hungry. Otherwise, aggression in the tank will skyrocket and they will go after fish, snails and other shrimp. Remove leftover food the next day to prevent contamination.

Some aquarists feed them directly, but this is not necessary unless there is high competition for food in the tank and a risk of the shrimp going hungry.

In the wild, like many other cleaner shrimp, they rely heavily on their clients for food. They perform a dancing behaviour: standing in a conspicuous spot on the reef, whipping their antennae while swaying from side to side. These areas are usually called cleaning stations. Many aquarists complain that they have never seen the shrimp clean fish. The reason is a conflict of interest: to make them clean the fish they must be very hungry, and you do not want them to be hungry in your tank.

These shrimp are great at keeping bristle worms (Polychaete) under control in a reef tank, which is one of the main reasons they became so popular.

They prefer the dark corners of a cave or ledges, so it is important to provide hiding places. They do best when they have somewhere to hide during the day.

Although coral banded shrimp are nocturnal, they can change their habits. According to a study, they can easily adapt physiologically and/or behaviourally to daylight and function as diurnal cleaner shrimp.

They can form pairs as juveniles and grow up together. Some guides say they pair for life, but this is not true. Biologists noticed that males and females form stable pairs for a long period, remaining together for at least two consecutive reproductive cycles, during which males follow and protect their female mates.

Environment plays a big role in their relationship. A pair that had been mixed for more than 2 weeks was observed to fight when moved to an unfamiliar aquarium. This was the only instance of fighting ever observed between an established pair.

They tend to be quite territorial. Pairs inhabit a restricted area and show strong aggression. They can be very aggressive against others of their own kind and are defensive when something comes within 1–2 metres of their area, especially another coral banded shrimp of the same sex, in which case they usually fight to the death. Among shrimp in aquaria there appeared to be no submissive or appeasement behaviour. Strange shrimp of the opposite sex tend to show initial fighting, followed by courtship and the formation of a breeding pair.

Reef safety: In general, coral banded shrimp are reef safe, but there are reports that they can nip at soft corals or anemones when hungry. They have their own personalities and their behaviour cannot be predicted: some live peacefully in reef tanks for years, others pinch at corals and anemones all the time. Keep an eye on them when you introduce them. In some cases they can accidentally damage coral while cleaning it and then eat the damaged part.

Tank mates: Avoid predatory fish big enough to eat them (triggerfish, larger hawkfish, groupers, lionfish and large predatory wrasses). However, in 1960 scientists observing adult Stenopus hispidus concluded that these shrimp did not seem to have any natural predators. The symbiosis between the shrimp and the reef community allows them to safely check the mouth and gills of a fish without being eaten. In another experiment, an octopus species that readily eats non-cleaner shrimp, crabs and lobsters did not eat the shrimp until it had gone without food for a few weeks. In a further experiment, a starved shrimp “danced” twice as often as a fed one, and the fish tried 11 times more often to engage with the shrimp.

It is not recommended to keep a coral banded shrimp with another of its kind, because they are very territorial, both in the wild and in captivity. The same applies to other Stenopus, even though they belong to different species. Keeping them with other shrimp such as red fire shrimp (Lysmata debelius), peppermint shrimp (Lysmata wurdemanni), skunk cleaner (Lysmata amboinensis), Saron shrimp, red-white cleaner shrimp and bumble bee shrimp is not recommended either. Some people manage it, but that does not mean it will work, as they can still be quite aggressive.

Because snails and hermit crabs are slow-moving, the risk of predation increases, so do not keep coral banded shrimp with snails and hermit crabs.

They are nocturnal, so it is important to have hiding places in the aquarium, and they do better on their own because of their aggression.

• Size: males are smaller than females.
  • Saddle and eggs: at all times of the year most females carry a large mass of green eggs attached to the underside of the abdomen, or a saddle.
  • The pleopods of the female, when folded close to the body, extend forward to the base of the second pereiopods. In males they extend only to the base of the fourth pereiopods.
  • A single, short, median spine is found on the underside of each abdominal segment of the male. These spines do not occur in females, except those less than 3 cm long.

Some of these criteria are very hard to see with the naked eye.

Mating usually occurs within 12–48 hours of a female molt, after which the female releases pheromones to attract the male. Females are more attractive to males within the first 24 hours after molting, and all matings at 12 and 24 hours after molting were successful. At 36 hours, only one out of four pairs mated successfully.

When ready to mate, the male performs a courting dance in front of the female. After antennule contact, the female stands with the abdomen raised, the male rapidly embraces the female abdomen to abdomen, then turns 150–180° to mate. The male does not bend around the body of the female. Copulation lasts only 5 to 10 seconds, and the male transfers a sperm sac to the female. The female starts spawning 15–25 minutes after successful mating, and spawning usually lasts about 10 minutes.

Many attempts have been made over the years to develop breeding technologies for this species, with little success. They are very difficult to breed in an aquarium because the larvae get eaten by other animals, get sucked into the filter, or simply die without proper nutrition or water parameters.

Females reach sexual maturity at 30 mm. They can produce from several hundred to over 2000 eggs per spawn, and clutch size increases approximately exponentially with female size from that point.

There are 4 stages of ovarian development, visible to the naked eye:

  • Spent ovary: translucent; lasts 3 days after spawning.
  • Developing ovary: milky-white; lasts 10 days after spawning.
  • Developed ovary: light green; between 10 and 18 days after spawning.
  • Advanced ovary: dark green.

After spawning, the eggs progress from heavily pigmented towards transparency. The colour of the egg mass gradually changes and eyespots appear 4 to 5 days before hatching.

Larvae typically hatch within 16 days of fertilisation at 28°C. Within 12 hours after hatching, the female can molt, mate and spawn again.

The young do not leave the mother immediately but stay attached to her for some time. Once detached, they float to the water surface.

Newly hatched larvae go through 9 larval stages before transforming into tiny copies of their parents. The larval period is long (at least 123 days), and larvae can delay metamorphosis for up to 210 days until suitable nutritional or environmental conditions are encountered. The young shrimp then settle on the bottom and find a dark place to hide.

Within the genus Stenopus there are 11 species. Although all are very similar, some have slight colour variations:

  • Blue (or Purple) banded coral shrimp (Stenopus tenuirostris)
  • Golden banded coral shrimp (Stenopus scutellatus)
  • Yellow banded coral shrimp (Stenopus zanzibaricus)

In all colour variations, the pincer arms and abdomen usually remain red and white striped.

The coral banded shrimp is known for its vibrant red and white stripes and the bands on its pincer claws. It is characterised by very long white antennae and antennules, bright red bars banding its white body, and enlarged, chelated third pereiopods. In captivity these shrimp usually reach 5–7 cm, although there are reports of up to 9 cm.
